case_info.scenario: A 46-year-old man presented with acute-onset weakness of his bilateral lower limbs for 3 days, accompanied by ascending numbness to just below his nipples. Three weeks prior, he had developed acute urinary retention. Neurological examination revealed weakness in bilateral lower limbs (Medical Research Council grade 4 on the right and grade 3 on the left), extensor plantar responses, and a sensory level at T6. Magnetic resonance imaging of his thoracic spine was performed 10 days after the onset of weakness and did not show any signal abnormalities or restricted diffusion. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis findings were remarkable for elevated protein (0.14 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]) but white cell count (5 cells/mm3) and glucose levels (54.05 mg/dL [to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.0555]) were normal. Cytology and flow cytometry were negative for malignancy. Antibodies to aquaporin 4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein were not detected. The patient developed a sudden worsening of weakness in his legs 2 weeks after initial presentation. Repeated thoracic spine imaging showed an area of T2 hyperintensity in the left posterolateral cord at T7, which did not enhance with contrast or show restricted diffusion (Figure 1A). Notably, he had a 4-year history of an asymptomatic papular skin eruption with more lesions developing in the last 4 months. These were distributed on the neck, trunk, and limbs, sparing his face, scalp, and genitalia (Figure 1B). Findings of extensive workup for malignancy, including full-body computed tomography scan, paraneoplastic antibody panel, and systemic autoimmune diseases (antinuclear antibody, antidouble stranded DNA, and myositis antibody panel), were negative. The skin papules were biopsied.
case_info.caption: T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thoracic spine showing an area of hyperintensity in the left posterolateral cord at T7 (A) (arrowhead). Multiple papules were seen on the patient’s abdomen. These consisted of hypopigmented papules with central hyperpigmented umbilication and larger papules with typical central atrophic porcelain white scarring (B).
case_info.explanation: The differential diagnoses to consider in a patient who has cutaneous papules and myelopathy can include infectious (eg, secondary syphilis, HIV), ischemic (eg, malignant atrophic papulosis), autoimmune (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet disease), and paraneoplastic (eg, scleromyxedema with paraproteinemia) causes. The diagnosis of malignant atrophic papulosis (MAP) or Köhlmeier-Degos disease was supported by the characteristic cutaneous eruption and histological findings of wedge-shaped dermal collagen degeneration, interstitial mucin deposition, small–vessel angiopathy with luminal thrombi, perivascular and perineural lymphocytic infiltration, and interface vacuolar alteration of the epidermis (Figure 2). These findings, indicative of microvascular injury, can also be seen in the setting of Degos-like diseases, namely dermatomyositis, lupus erythematosus, and scleroderma. Negative autoimmune markers and the absence of characteristic clinical features excluded these differential diagnoses. Scleromyxedema is an unusual condition of dermal mucin deposition and fibroblast proliferation and is typically associated with a monoclonal gammopathy and other systemic manifestations. Histopathological findings of microvascular injury in the patient are not consistent with this diagnosis. Lues maligna is a rare but severe form of secondary syphilis that has been described in patients who have HIV co-infection—cutaneous lesions start out as papules that ulcerate to become well-demarcated necrotic plaques. Syphilis was ruled out with negative findings on serum, cerebrospinal fluid treponemal, and nontreponemal antibody tests, and the absence of spirochetes on skin biopsy. The acute and stepwise deterioration of this patient’s thoracic myelopathy is consistent with a vascular event. MAP is a thrombo-occlusive microangiopathy predominantly targeting the skin, gastrointestinal system, and central nervous system (CNS), with poorly understood pathogenesis. A seminal article found vascular C5b-9 and high expression of interferon-α in all skin, gastrointestinal, and CNS tissue samples, and concluded that a dysregulated interferon-α response in concert with membranolytic attack complex deposition contributed to unique vascular injuries.1In the largest series of patients who had neurologic manifestations of MAP, fatal hemorrhagic or ischemic strokes and a disabling polyradiculoneuropathy were described.2Vascular cord lesions have been less commonly reported, but patchy involvement of the entire transverse section of the cord may explain why clinically manifested lesions may not appear on imaging.3,4The long-term prognosis of MAP is poor with a high mortality rate, most commonly from bowel perforation.5 Expert opinion supports the use of antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy.6Response to conventional immunosuppression has been inconsistent,2and the use of corticosteroids has been associated with a risk of intestinal perforation.6Intravenous immunoglobulin was found to be useful in a case report of MAP with neurological involvement.7Eculizumab, a monoclonal anti-C5 antibody, has shown some success in MAP with gastrointestinal involvement.8 The patient received aspirin, clopidogrel, and intravenous immunoglobulin infusion (2 mg/kg) with no further neurological deterioration. He was also treated with baricitinib at 4 mg daily. Baricitinib is a Janus kinase inhibitor, approved for use in rheumatoid arthritis refractory to tumor necrosis factor inhibitors. It modulates the immune system through the inhibition of cytokine activity, and the therapeutic choice was made with the aim of controlling interferon-α–mediated vascular damage. Notably, baricitinib has high CNS penetration with reported cerebrospinal fluid serologic plasma ratios of 20% in mouse studies and has been repurposed for COVID-19 infections to reduce virus-induced neurological damage.9 This case highlights the rare but important neurological complication of MAP. Future research will help clarify the pathogenesis and allow novel pathogenesis directed therapy in this otherwise lethal disease.

Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Clinical case]
A 46-year-old man presented with acute-onset weakness of his bilateral lower limbs for 3 days, accompanied by ascending numbness to just below his nipples. Three weeks prior, he had developed acute urinary retention. Neurological examination revealed weakness in bilateral lower limbs (Medical Research Council grade 4 on the right and grade 3 on the left), extensor plantar responses, and a sensory level at T6. Magnetic resonance imaging of his thoracic spine was performed 10 days after the onset of weakness and did not show any signal abnormalities or restricted diffusion. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis findings were remarkable for elevated protein (0.14 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]) but white cell count (5 cells/mm3) and glucose levels (54.05 mg/dL [to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.0555]) were normal. Cytology and flow cytometry were negative for malignancy. Antibodies to aquaporin 4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein were not detected. The patient developed a sudden worsening of weakness in his legs 2 weeks after initial presentation. Repeated thoracic spine imaging showed an area of T2 hyperintensity in the left posterolateral cord at T7, which did not enhance with contrast or show restricted diffusion (Figure 1A). Notably, he had a 4-year history of an asymptomatic papular skin eruption with more lesions developing in the last 4 months. These were distributed on the neck, trunk, and limbs, sparing his face, scalp, and genitalia (Figure 1B). Findings of extensive workup for malignancy, including full-body computed tomography scan, paraneoplastic antibody panel, and systemic autoimmune diseases (antinuclear antibody, antidouble stranded DNA, and myositis antibody panel), were negative. The skin papules were biopsied.

case_info.explanation: The differential diagnoses to consider in a patient who has cutaneous papules and myelopathy can include infectious (eg, secondary syphilis, HIV), ischemic (eg, malignant atrophic papulosis), autoimmune (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet disease), and paraneoplastic (eg, scleromyxedema with paraproteinemia) causes. The diagnosis of malignant atrophic papulosis (MAP) or Köhlmeier-Degos disease was supported by the characteristic cutaneous eruption and histological findings of wedge-shaped dermal collagen degeneration, interstitial mucin deposition, small–vessel angiopathy with luminal thrombi, perivascular and perineural lymphocytic infiltration, and interface vacuolar alteration of the epidermis (Figure 2). These findings, indicative of microvascular injury, can also be seen in the setting of Degos-like diseases, namely dermatomyositis, lupus erythematosus, and scleroderma. Negative autoimmune markers and the absence of characteristic clinical features excluded these differential diagnoses. Scleromyxedema is an unusual condition of dermal mucin deposition and fibroblast proliferation and is typically associated with a monoclonal gammopathy and other systemic manifestations. Histopathological findings of microvascular injury in the patient are not consistent with this diagnosis. Lues maligna is a rare but severe form of secondary syphilis that has been described in patients who have HIV co-infection—cutaneous lesions start out as papules that ulcerate to become well-demarcated necrotic plaques. Syphilis was ruled out with negative findings on serum, cerebrospinal fluid treponemal, and nontreponemal antibody tests, and the absence of spirochetes on skin biopsy. The acute and stepwise deterioration of this patient’s thoracic myelopathy is consistent with a vascular event. MAP is a thrombo-occlusive microangiopathy predominantly targeting the skin, gastrointestinal system, and central nervous system (CNS), with poorly understood pathogenesis. A seminal article found vascular C5b-9 and high expression of interferon-α in all skin, gastrointestinal, and CNS tissue samples, and concluded that a dysregulated interferon-α response in concert with membranolytic attack complex deposition contributed to unique vascular injuries.1In the largest series of patients who had neurologic manifestations of MAP, fatal hemorrhagic or ischemic strokes and a disabling polyradiculoneuropathy were described.2Vascular cord lesions have been less commonly reported, but patchy involvement of the entire transverse section of the cord may explain why clinically manifested lesions may not appear on imaging.3,4The long-term prognosis of MAP is poor with a high mortality rate, most commonly from bowel perforation.5 Expert opinion supports the use of antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy.6Response to conventional immunosuppression has been inconsistent,2and the use of corticosteroids has been associated with a risk of intestinal perforation.6Intravenous immunoglobulin was found to be useful in a case report of MAP with neurological involvement.7Eculizumab, a monoclonal anti-C5 antibody, has shown some success in MAP with gastrointestinal involvement.8 The patient received aspirin, clopidogrel, and intravenous immunoglobulin infusion (2 mg/kg) with no further neurological deterioration. He was also treated with baricitinib at 4 mg daily. Baricitinib is a Janus kinase inhibitor, approved for use in rheumatoid arthritis refractory to tumor necrosis factor inhibitors. It modulates the immune system through the inhibition of cytokine activity, and the therapeutic choice was made with the aim of controlling interferon-α–mediated vascular damage. Notably, baricitinib has high CNS penetration with reported cerebrospinal fluid serologic plasma ratios of 20% in mouse studies and has been repurposed for COVID-19 infections to reduce virus-induced neurological damage.9 This case highlights the rare but important neurological complication of MAP. Future research will help clarify the pathogenesis and allow novel pathogenesis directed therapy in this otherwise lethal disease.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 46-year-old man presented with acute-onset weakness of his bilateral lower limbs for 3 days, accompanied by ascending numbness to just below his nipples. Three weeks prior, he had developed acute urinary retention. Neurological examination revealed weakness in bilateral lower limbs (Medical Research Council grade 4 on the right and grade 3 on the left), extensor plantar responses, and a sensory level at T6. Cytology and flow cytometry were negative for malignancy. Antibodies to aquaporin 4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein were not detected. The patient developed a sudden worsening of weakness in his legs 2 weeks after initial presentation. Repeated thoracic spine imaging showed an area of T2 hyperintensity in the left posterolateral cord at T7, which did not enhance with contrast or show restricted diffusion (Figure 1A). Notably, he had a 4-year history of an asymptomatic papular skin eruption with more lesions developing in the last 4 months. These were distributed on the neck, trunk, and limbs, sparing his face, scalp, and genitalia (Figure 1B). Findings of extensive workup for malignancy, including full-body computed tomography scan, paraneoplastic antibody panel, and systemic autoimmune diseases (antinuclear antibody, antidouble stranded DNA, and myositis antibody panel), were negative. The skin papules were biopsied.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

[Output Format]

  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 3.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"

case_info.explanation: The differential diagnoses to consider in a patient who has cutaneous papules and myelopathy can include infectious (eg, secondary syphilis, HIV), ischemic (eg, malignant atrophic papulosis), autoimmune (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet disease), and paraneoplastic (eg, scleromyxedema with paraproteinemia) causes. The diagnosis of malignant atrophic papulosis (MAP) or Köhlmeier-Degos disease was supported by the characteristic cutaneous eruption and histological findings of wedge-shaped dermal collagen degeneration, interstitial mucin deposition, small–vessel angiopathy with luminal thrombi, perivascular and perineural lymphocytic infiltration, and interface vacuolar alteration of the epidermis (Figure 2). These findings, indicative of microvascular injury, can also be seen in the setting of Degos-like diseases, namely dermatomyositis, lupus erythematosus, and scleroderma. Negative autoimmune markers and the absence of characteristic clinical features excluded these differential diagnoses. Scleromyxedema is an unusual condition of dermal mucin deposition and fibroblast proliferation and is typically associated with a monoclonal gammopathy and other systemic manifestations. Histopathological findings of microvascular injury in the patient are not consistent with this diagnosis. Lues maligna is a rare but severe form of secondary syphilis that has been described in patients who have HIV co-infection—cutaneous lesions start out as papules that ulcerate to become well-demarcated necrotic plaques. Syphilis was ruled out with negative findings on serum, cerebrospinal fluid treponemal, and nontreponemal antibody tests, and the absence of spirochetes on skin biopsy. The acute and stepwise deterioration of this patient’s thoracic myelopathy is consistent with a vascular event. MAP is a thrombo-occlusive microangiopathy predominantly targeting the skin, gastrointestinal system, and central nervous system (CNS), with poorly understood pathogenesis. A seminal article found vascular C5b-9 and high expression of interferon-α in all skin, gastrointestinal, and CNS tissue samples, and concluded that a dysregulated interferon-α response in concert with membranolytic attack complex deposition contributed to unique vascular injuries.1In the largest series of patients who had neurologic manifestations of MAP, fatal hemorrhagic or ischemic strokes and a disabling polyradiculoneuropathy were described.2Vascular cord lesions have been less commonly reported, but patchy involvement of the entire transverse section of the cord may explain why clinically manifested lesions may not appear on imaging.3,4The long-term prognosis of MAP is poor with a high mortality rate, most commonly from bowel perforation.5 Expert opinion supports the use of antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy.6Response to conventional immunosuppression has been inconsistent,2and the use of corticosteroids has been associated with a risk of intestinal perforation.6Intravenous immunoglobulin was found to be useful in a case report of MAP with neurological involvement.7Eculizumab, a monoclonal anti-C5 antibody, has shown some success in MAP with gastrointestinal involvement.8 The patient received aspirin, clopidogrel, and intravenous immunoglobulin infusion (2 mg/kg) with no further neurological deterioration. He was also treated with baricitinib at 4 mg daily. Baricitinib is a Janus kinase inhibitor, approved for use in rheumatoid arthritis refractory to tumor necrosis factor inhibitors. It modulates the immune system through the inhibition of cytokine activity, and the therapeutic choice was made with the aim of controlling interferon-α–mediated vascular damage. Notably, baricitinib has high CNS penetration with reported cerebrospinal fluid serologic plasma ratios of 20% in mouse studies and has been repurposed for COVID-19 infections to reduce virus-induced neurological damage.9 This case highlights the rare but important neurological complication of MAP. Future research will help clarify the pathogenesis and allow novel pathogenesis directed therapy in this otherwise lethal disease.

These were distributed on the neck, trunk, and limbs, sparing his face, scalp, and genitalia (Figure 1B). Findings of extensive workup for malignancy, including full-body computed tomography scan, paraneoplastic antibody panel, and systemic autoimmune diseases (antinuclear antibody, antidouble stranded DNA, and myositis antibody panel), were negative. The skin papules were biopsied.

case_info.explanation: The differential diagnoses to consider in a patient who has cutaneous papules and myelopathy can include infectious (eg, secondary syphilis, HIV), ischemic (eg, malignant atrophic papulosis), autoimmune (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet disease), and paraneoplastic (eg, scleromyxedema with paraproteinemia) causes. The diagnosis of malignant atrophic papulosis (MAP) or Köhlmeier-Degos disease was supported by the characteristic cutaneous eruption and histological findings of wedge-shaped dermal collagen degeneration, interstitial mucin deposition, small–vessel angiopathy with luminal thrombi, perivascular and perineural lymphocytic infiltration, and interface vacuolar alteration of the epidermis (Figure 2). These findings, indicative of microvascular injury, can also be seen in the setting of Degos-like diseases, namely dermatomyositis, lupus erythematosus, and scleroderma. Negative autoimmune markers and the absence of characteristic clinical features excluded these differential diagnoses. Scleromyxedema is an unusual condition of dermal mucin deposition and fibroblast proliferation and is typically associated with a monoclonal gammopathy and other systemic manifestations. Histopathological findings of microvascular injury in the patient are not consistent with this diagnosis. Lues maligna is a rare but severe form of secondary syphilis that has been described in patients who have HIV co-infection—cutaneous lesions start out as papules that ulcerate to become well-demarcated necrotic plaques. You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 46-year-old man presented with acute-onset weakness of his bilateral lower limbs for 3 days, accompanied by ascending numbness to just below his nipples. Three weeks prior, he had developed acute urinary retention. Neurological examination revealed weakness in bilateral lower limbs (Medical Research Council grade 4 on the right and grade 3 on the left), extensor plantar responses, and a sensory level at T6. Magnetic resonance imaging of his thoracic spine was performed 10 days after the onset of weakness and did not show any signal abnormalities or restricted diffusion. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis findings were remarkable for elevated protein (0.14 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]) but white cell count (5 cells/mm3) and glucose levels (54.05 mg/dL [to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.0555]) were normal. Cytology and flow cytometry were negative for malignancy. Antibodies to aquaporin 4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein were not detected. The patient developed a sudden worsening of weakness in his legs 2 weeks after initial presentation. Repeated thoracic spine imaging showed an area of T2 hyperintensity in the left posterolateral cord at T7, which did not enhance with contrast or show restricted diffusion (Figure 1A). Notably, he had a 4-year history of an asymptomatic papular skin eruption with more lesions developing in the last 4 months. These were distributed on the neck, trunk, and limbs, sparing his face, scalp, and genitalia (Figure 1B). Findings of extensive workup for malignancy, including full-body computed tomography scan, paraneoplastic antibody panel, and systemic autoimmune diseases (antinuclear antibody, antidouble stranded DNA, and myositis antibody panel), were negative. The skin papules were biopsied.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 7.7. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,
  "performance": <integer 1-5>,

  "frustration": <integer 1-5>,

case_info.explanation: The differential diagnoses to consider in a patient who has cutaneous papules and myelopathy can include infectious (eg, secondary syphilis, HIV), ischemic (eg, malignant atrophic papulosis), autoimmune (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet disease), and paraneoplastic (eg, scleromyxedema with paraproteinemia) causes. The diagnosis of malignant atrophic papulosis (MAP) or Köhlmeier-Degos disease was supported by the characteristic cutaneous eruption and histological findings of wedge-shaped dermal collagen degeneration, interstitial mucin deposition, small–vessel angiopathy with luminal thrombi, perivascular and perineural lymphocytic infiltration, and interface vacuolar alteration of the epidermis (Figure 2). These findings, indicative of microvascular injury, can also be seen in the setting of Degos-like diseases, namely dermatomyositis, lupus erythematosus, and scleroderma. Negative autoimmune markers and the absence of characteristic clinical features excluded these differential diagnoses. Scleromyxedema is an unusual condition of dermal mucin deposition and fibroblast proliferation and is typically associated with a monoclonal gammopathy and other systemic manifestations. Histopathological findings of microvascular injury in the patient are not consistent with this diagnosis. Lues maligna is a rare but severe form of secondary syphilis that has been described in patients who have HIV co-infection—cutaneous lesions start out as papules that ulcerate to become well-demarcated necrotic plaques. Syphilis was ruled out with negative findings on serum, cerebrospinal fluid treponemal, and nontreponemal antibody tests, and the absence of spirochetes on skin biopsy. The acute and stepwise deterioration of this patient’s thoracic myelopathy is consistent with a vascular event. MAP is a thrombo-occlusive microangiopathy predominantly targeting the skin, gastrointestinal system, and central nervous system (CNS), with poorly understood pathogenesis. A seminal article found vascular C5b-9 and high expression of interferon-α in all skin, gastrointestinal, and CNS tissue samples, and concluded that a dysregulated interferon-α response in concert with membranolytic attack complex deposition contributed to unique vascular injuries.1In the largest series of patients who had neurologic manifestations of MAP, fatal hemorrhagic or ischemic strokes and a disabling polyradiculoneuropathy were described.2Vascular cord lesions have been less commonly reported, but patchy involvement of the entire transverse section of the cord may explain why clinically manifested lesions may not appear on imaging.3,4The long-term prognosis of MAP is poor with a high mortality rate, most commonly from bowel perforation.5 Expert opinion supports the use of antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy.6Response to conventional immunosuppression has been inconsistent,2and the use of corticosteroids has been associated with a risk of intestinal perforation.6Intravenous immunoglobulin was found to be useful in a case report of MAP with neurological involvement.7Eculizumab, a monoclonal anti-C5 antibody, has shown some success in MAP with gastrointestinal involvement.8 The patient received aspirin, clopidogrel, and intravenous immunoglobulin infusion (2 mg/kg) with no further neurological deterioration. He was also treated with baricitinib at 4 mg daily. Baricitinib is a Janus kinase inhibitor, approved for use in rheumatoid arthritis refractory to tumor necrosis factor inhibitors. It modulates the immune system through the inhibition of cytokine activity, and the therapeutic choice was made with the aim of controlling interferon-α–mediated vascular damage. Notably, baricitinib has high CNS penetration with reported cerebrospinal fluid serologic plasma ratios of 20% in mouse studies and has been repurposed for COVID-19 infections to reduce virus-induced neurological damage.9 This case highlights the rare but important neurological complication of MAP. Future research will help clarify the pathogenesis and allow novel pathogenesis directed therapy in this otherwise lethal disease.

case_info.explanation: The differential diagnoses to consider in a patient who has cutaneous papules and myelopathy can include infectious (eg, secondary syphilis, HIV), ischemic (eg, malignant atrophic papulosis), autoimmune (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet disease), and paraneoplastic (eg, scleromyxedema with paraproteinemia) causes. The diagnosis of malignant atrophic papulosis (MAP) or Köhlmeier-Degos disease was supported by the characteristic cutaneous eruption and histological findings of wedge-shaped dermal collagen degeneration, interstitial mucin deposition, small–vessel angiopathy with luminal thrombi, perivascular and perineural lymphocytic infiltration, and interface vacuolar alteration of the epidermis (Figure 2). These findings, indicative of microvascular injury, can also be seen in the setting of Degos-like diseases, namely dermatomyositis, lupus erythematosus, and scleroderma. Negative autoimmune markers and the absence of characteristic clinical features excluded these differential diagnoses. Scleromyxedema is an unusual condition of dermal mucin deposition and fibroblast proliferation and is typically associated with a monoclonal gammopathy and other systemic manifestations. Histopathological findings of microvascular injury in the patient are not consistent with this diagnosis. Lues maligna is a rare but severe form of secondary syphilis that has been described in patients who have HIV co-infection—cutaneous lesions start out as papules that ulcerate to become well-demarcated necrotic plaques. Syphilis was ruled out with negative findings on serum, cerebrospinal fluid treponemal, and nontreponemal antibody tests, and the absence of spirochetes on skin biopsy. The acute and stepwise deterioration of this patient’s thoracic myelopathy is consistent with a vascular event. MAP is a thrombo-occlusive microangiopathy predominantly targeting the skin, gastrointestinal system, and central nervous system (CNS), with poorly understood pathogenesis. A seminal article found vascular C5b-9 and high expression of interferon-α in all skin, gastrointestinal, and CNS tissue samples, and concluded that a dysregulated interferon-α response in concert with membranolytic attack complex deposition contributed to unique vascular injuries.1In the largest series of patients who had neurologic manifestations of MAP, fatal hemorrhagic or ischemic strokes and a disabling polyradiculoneuropathy were described.2Vascular cord lesions have been less commonly reported, but patchy involvement of the entire transverse section of the cord may explain why clinically manifested lesions may not appear on imaging.3,4The long-term prognosis of MAP is poor with a high mortality rate, most commonly from bowel perforation.5 Expert opinion supports the use of antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy.6Response to conventional immunosuppression has been inconsistent,2and the use of corticosteroids has been associated with a risk of intestinal perforation.6Intravenous immunoglobulin was found to be useful in a case report of MAP with neurological involvement.7Eculizumab, a monoclonal anti-C5 antibody, has shown some success in MAP with gastrointestinal involvement.8 The patient received aspirin, clopidogrel, and intravenous immunoglobulin infusion (2 mg/kg) with no further neurological deterioration. He was also treated with baricitinib at 4 mg daily. Baricitinib is a Janus kinase inhibitor, approved for use in rheumatoid arthritis refractory to tumor necrosis factor inhibitors. It modulates the immune system through the inhibition of cytokine activity, and the therapeutic choice was made with the aim of controlling interferon-α–mediated vascular damage. Notably, baricitinib has high CNS penetration with reported cerebrospinal fluid serologic plasma ratios of 20% in mouse studies and has been repurposed for COVID-19 infections to reduce virus-induced neurological damage.9 This case highlights the rare but important neurological complication of MAP. Future research will help clarify the pathogenesis and allow novel pathogenesis directed therapy in this otherwise lethal disease.

Three weeks prior, he had developed acute urinary retention. Neurological examination revealed weakness in bilateral lower limbs (Medical Research Council grade 4 on the right and grade 3 on the left), extensor plantar responses, and a sensory level at T6. case_info.caption: T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thoracic spine showing an area of hyperintensity in the left posterolateral cord at T7 (A) (arrowhead). Multiple papules were seen on the patient’s abdomen. These consisted of hypopigmented papules with central hyperpigmented umbilication and larger papules with typical central atrophic porcelain white scarring (B).
case_info.explanation: The differential diagnoses to consider in a patient who has cutaneous papules and myelopathy can include infectious (eg, secondary syphilis, HIV), ischemic (eg, malignant atrophic papulosis), autoimmune (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet disease), and paraneoplastic (eg, scleromyxedema with paraproteinemia) causes. The diagnosis of malignant atrophic papulosis (MAP) or Köhlmeier-Degos disease was supported by the characteristic cutaneous eruption and histological findings of wedge-shaped dermal collagen degeneration, interstitial mucin deposition, small–vessel angiopathy with luminal thrombi, perivascular and perineural lymphocytic infiltration, and interface vacuolar alteration of the epidermis (Figure 2). These findings, indicative of microvascular injury, can also be seen in the setting of Degos-like diseases, namely dermatomyositis, lupus erythematosus, and scleroderma. Negative autoimmune markers and the absence of characteristic clinical features excluded these differential diagnoses. Scleromyxedema is an unusual condition of dermal mucin deposition and fibroblast proliferation and is typically associated with a monoclonal gammopathy and other systemic manifestations. Histopathological findings of microvascular injury in the patient are not consistent with this diagnosis. Lues maligna is a rare but severe form of secondary syphilis that has been described in patients who have HIV co-infection—cutaneous lesions start out as papules that ulcerate to become well-demarcated necrotic plaques. Syphilis was ruled out with negative findings on serum, cerebrospinal fluid treponemal, and nontreponemal antibody tests, and the absence of spirochetes on skin biopsy. The acute and stepwise deterioration of this patient’s thoracic myelopathy is consistent with a vascular event. MAP is a thrombo-occlusive microangiopathy predominantly targeting the skin, gastrointestinal system, and central nervous system (CNS), with poorly understood pathogenesis. A seminal article found vascular C5b-9 and high expression of interferon-α in all skin, gastrointestinal, and CNS tissue samples, and concluded that a dysregulated interferon-α response in concert with membranolytic attack complex deposition contributed to unique vascular injuries.1In the largest series of patients who had neurologic manifestations of MAP, fatal hemorrhagic or ischemic strokes and a disabling polyradiculoneuropathy were described.2Vascular cord lesions have been less commonly reported, but patchy involvement of the entire transverse section of the cord may explain why clinically manifested lesions may not appear on imaging.3,4The long-term prognosis of MAP is poor with a high mortality rate, most commonly from bowel perforation.5 Expert opinion supports the use of antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy.6Response to conventional immunosuppression has been inconsistent,2and the use of corticosteroids has been associated with a risk of intestinal perforation.6Intravenous immunoglobulin was found to be useful in a case report of MAP with neurological involvement.7Eculizumab, a monoclonal anti-C5 antibody, has shown some success in MAP with gastrointestinal involvement.8 The patient received aspirin, clopidogrel, and intravenous immunoglobulin infusion (2 mg/kg) with no further neurological deterioration. He was also treated with baricitinib at 4 mg daily. Baricitinib is a Janus kinase inhibitor, approved for use in rheumatoid arthritis refractory to tumor necrosis factor inhibitors. It modulates the immune system through the inhibition of cytokine activity, and the therapeutic choice was made with the aim of controlling interferon-α–mediated vascular damage. Notably, baricitinib has high CNS penetration with reported cerebrospinal fluid serologic plasma ratios of 20% in mouse studies and has been repurposed for COVID-19 infections to reduce virus-induced neurological damage.9 This case highlights the rare but important neurological complication of MAP. Future research will help clarify the pathogenesis and allow novel pathogenesis directed therapy in this otherwise lethal disease.

case_info.scenario: A 46-year-old man presented with acute-onset weakness of his bilateral lower limbs for 3 days, accompanied by ascending numbness to just below his nipples. Three weeks prior, he had developed acute urinary retention. Neurological examination revealed weakness in bilateral lower limbs (Medical Research Council grade 4 on the right and grade 3 on the left), extensor plantar responses, and a sensory level at T6. Magnetic resonance imaging of his thoracic spine was performed 10 days after the onset of weakness and did not show any signal abnormalities or restricted diffusion. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis findings were remarkable for elevated protein (0.14 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]) but white cell count (5 cells/mm3) and glucose levels (54.05 mg/dL [to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.0555]) were normal. Cytology and flow cytometry were negative for malignancy. Antibodies to aquaporin 4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein were not detected. The patient developed a sudden worsening of weakness in his legs 2 weeks after initial presentation. Repeated thoracic spine imaging showed an area of T2 hyperintensity in the left posterolateral cord at T7, which did not enhance with contrast or show restricted diffusion (Figure 1A). Notably, he had a 4-year history of an asymptomatic papular skin eruption with more lesions developing in the last 4 months. These were distributed on the neck, trunk, and limbs, sparing his face, scalp, and genitalia (Figure 1B). Findings of extensive workup for malignancy, including full-body computed tomography scan, paraneoplastic antibody panel, and systemic autoimmune diseases (antinuclear antibody, antidouble stranded DNA, and myositis antibody panel), were negative. The skin papules were biopsied.
case_info.caption: T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thoracic spine showing an area of hyperintensity in the left posterolateral cord at T7 (A) (arrowhead). Multiple papules were seen on the patient’s abdomen. These consisted of hypopigmented papules with central hyperpigmented umbilication and larger papules with typical central atrophic porcelain white scarring (B).
case_info.explanation: The differential diagnoses to consider in a patient who has cutaneous papules and myelopathy can include infectious (eg, secondary syphilis, HIV), ischemic (eg, malignant atrophic papulosis), autoimmune (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet disease), and paraneoplastic (eg, scleromyxedema with paraproteinemia) causes. The diagnosis of malignant atrophic papulosis (MAP) or Köhlmeier-Degos disease was supported by the characteristic cutaneous eruption and histological findings of wedge-shaped dermal collagen degeneration, interstitial mucin deposition, small–vessel angiopathy with luminal thrombi, perivascular and perineural lymphocytic infiltration, and interface vacuolar alteration of the epidermis (Figure 2). These findings, indicative of microvascular injury, can also be seen in the setting of Degos-like diseases, namely dermatomyositis, lupus erythematosus, and scleroderma. Negative autoimmune markers and the absence of characteristic clinical features excluded these differential diagnoses. Scleromyxedema is an unusual condition of dermal mucin deposition and fibroblast proliferation and is typically associated with a monoclonal gammopathy and other systemic manifestations. Histopathological findings of microvascular injury in the patient are not consistent with this diagnosis. Lues maligna is a rare but severe form of secondary syphilis that has been described in patients who have HIV co-infection—cutaneous lesions start out as papules that ulcerate to become well-demarcated necrotic plaques. Syphilis was ruled out with negative findings on serum, cerebrospinal fluid treponemal, and nontreponemal antibody tests, and the absence of spirochetes on skin biopsy. The acute and stepwise deterioration of this patient’s thoracic myelopathy is consistent with a vascular event. MAP is a thrombo-occlusive microangiopathy predominantly targeting the skin, gastrointestinal system, and central nervous system (CNS), with poorly understood pathogenesis. A seminal article found vascular C5b-9 and high expression of interferon-α in all skin, gastrointestinal, and CNS tissue samples, and concluded that a dysregulated interferon-α response in concert with membranolytic attack complex deposition contributed to unique vascular injuries.1In the largest series of patients who had neurologic manifestations of MAP, fatal hemorrhagic or ischemic strokes and a disabling polyradiculoneuropathy were described.2Vascular cord lesions have been less commonly reported, but patchy involvement of the entire transverse section of the cord may explain why clinically manifested lesions may not appear on imaging.3,4The long-term prognosis of MAP is poor with a high mortality rate, most commonly from bowel perforation.5 Expert opinion supports the use of antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy.6Response to conventional immunosuppression has been inconsistent,2and the use of corticosteroids has been associated with a risk of intestinal perforation.6Intravenous immunoglobulin was found to be useful in a case report of MAP with neurological involvement.7Eculizumab, a monoclonal anti-C5 antibody, has shown some success in MAP with gastrointestinal involvement.8 The patient received aspirin, clopidogrel, and intravenous immunoglobulin infusion (2 mg/kg) with no further neurological deterioration. He was also treated with baricitinib at 4 mg daily. Baricitinib is a Janus kinase inhibitor, approved for use in rheumatoid arthritis refractory to tumor necrosis factor inhibitors. It modulates the immune system through the inhibition of cytokine activity, and the therapeutic choice was made with the aim of controlling interferon-α–mediated vascular damage. Notably, baricitinib has high CNS penetration with reported cerebrospinal fluid serologic plasma ratios of 20% in mouse studies and has been repurposed for COVID-19 infections to reduce virus-induced neurological damage.9 This case highlights the rare but important neurological complication of MAP. Future research will help clarify the pathogenesis and allow novel pathogenesis directed therapy in this otherwise lethal disease.
